about: What Town Meeting voted for every town department, and which departments move the total.

conclusions.basis: The twelve group totals the FY2025 omnibus prints, as shares of the grand total on the same page.
conclusions.claim: More than half the town budget is the schools, and four departments are five sixths of it
conclusions.detail: Before any question about growth: this is how one voted budget divides between the twelve departments that share it. Schools takes 57.1% of the FY2025 voted budget. Adding Protection, employee benefits and debt service brings four departments to 84.1% of the whole. The largest department is 313 times the size of the smallest.

ratio.unit: times: the largest department against the smallest

share.unit: of the voted budget, the school line

conclusions.not_shown: What any department buys with it, or how many people it employs.
conclusions.so_what: Most of what the town votes on is one department, and most of the rest is three.

conclusions.basis: The twelve group totals each omnibus prints, FY2023 against FY2025.
conclusions.claim: Ten of the twelve departments grew faster than the levy cap, not one of them
conclusions.detail: Every department in the voted budget except Central Purchasing and debt service outgrew the 2.5% the levy may rise by. Across the three years the town publishes department detail for, 10 of 12 departments grew faster than 2.5% a year. Only Central Purchasing, which is nearly flat, and maturing debt, which falls as bonds are paid off, did not. The budget rose 2.9% a year in total over the same period.
conclusions.not_shown: Why any of them grew. An amount voted gives no reason for itself.
conclusions.so_what: An argument about one department is an argument about part of the problem.

conclusions.basis: Total Schools against the other eleven group totals, FY2023 to FY2025.
conclusions.claim: The schools are the biggest line in the budget and not the fastest growing one
conclusions.detail: At 57.1% of the budget the school line dominates the total, but eight departments grew faster than it did. The school appropriation grew 3.6% a year across the three years, which is slower than eight of the eleven departments that grew at all. What grew fastest of the large lines is employee benefits and reserves — seven tenths of it group health insurance — at 12.7% a year.
conclusions.not_shown: What the school line buys, or whether it kept buying the same things.
conclusions.so_what: Size and growth are different questions and the school line answers them differently.

conclusions.basis: Each group’s own FY2025 figure times how far its growth exceeds the levy cap — dollars a year, not an index.
conclusions.claim: Employee benefits move the total more than the schools do
conclusions.detail: Weight times excess growth, not weight alone: a small line growing fast can push the total harder than a huge line growing slowly. Employee benefits and reserves are 9.8% of the voted budget and grew 12.7% a year, which is $438,870 a year more than the levy cap would carry. The schools are 57.1% of it and grew more slowly, at $284,306 a year above the cap. The smaller line does more of the pushing, and seven tenths of it is group health insurance.

spull.unit: a year above the cap, from the schools

tpull.unit: a year above the cap, from employee benefits

conclusions.not_shown: How much of the health insurance is school staff. The budget does not split it.
conclusions.so_what: Ranking departments by size points at the wrong one to ask questions about.

conclusions.basis: Total Maturing Debt in the FY2023 and FY2025 omnibus budgets.
conclusions.claim: Debt service fell by a third and the budget still grew — the room was absorbed
conclusions.detail: Maturing debt and interest is the only line in the voted budget that falls, and it falls a long way. Debt service fell from $4,497,723 to $2,941,322 across the three years, freeing $1,556,402 a year. The total still rose, so the room the roll-off created went to other lines rather than to the levy.

freed.unit: a year freed by debt rolling off

conclusions.not_shown: Which lines the freed money went to. The budget does not trace it.
conclusions.so_what: Debt coming off a budget is real room, and it is already spent here.

conclusions.basis: The twelve group totals, FY2023 against FY2025, aggregated three ways.
conclusions.claim: Take retiring debt out and the town side grew more than twice as fast as the schools
conclusions.detail: The non-school budget looks restrained until you notice that most of its restraint is bonds being paid off rather than anything anybody decided. Everything except the schools grew 2.0% a year — below the levy cap, and a figure that invites the conclusion the town side held the line. It did not: that average contains debt service falling as bonds retire. Debt is not a service. Excluding it, the rest of the town grew 8.0% a year against the schools’ 3.6%.

non.unit: a year, everything but the schools

nond.unit: a year, once retiring debt is taken out

conclusions.not_shown: Why the town side grew. This says where the money went, not what it bought or whether anybody got more of anything.
conclusions.so_what: An average that contains debt rolling off will understate every service in it.

conclusions.basis: The printed grand total of every omnibus, FY2012 to FY2025, and Article 10 of the 3 May 2025 Annual Town Meeting for FY2026.
conclusions.claim: The largest rise in fifteen years is also the first year with no detail published
conclusions.detail: FY2026 is a single number. The table that would show which departments it went to is not printed anywhere in the report. The voted budget rose 12.2% into FY2026, the largest one-year rise in the series that starts in FY2012. It is also the first year the annual report prints no department figures at all — Article 10 appears as prose, and the appropriations schedule that ran through FY2023 has stopped too.

rise.unit: in one year, the largest since FY2012

conclusions.not_shown: Which departments the rise went to. That is the figure that is missing.
conclusions.so_what: The year worth explaining is the year the town stopped publishing the explanation.

grain: DOLLARS VOTED at Town Meeting, in the omnibus budget for the year ahead. Not what any department requested, not what it spent, and not a service level. A voted budget is already balanced, so it records who absorbed the pressure rather than who is short.
not_established: What any department ASKED for. The omnibus is what Town Meeting voted, which is already balanced — the difference between a request and a vote is where a cut lives, and the annual report prints only the second.
What was actually spent. Voted and spent are different quantities and rule 1 forbids mixing them in one calculation.
Whether any department reduced SERVICE. A department can hold its dollars and cut its hours, and a dollar figure will not say so.
Why any line moved. The omnibus states an amount and gives no reason for it, so every explanation of a movement here would be a hypothesis.
Anything about FY2026 below the total. The FY2025 annual report prints no department figures at all.

That growing faster than the levy cap is a problem. Proposition 2½ limits the LEVY, not the budget: the budget is the levy plus state aid, local receipts and transfers, and new growth raises the levy limit on top of the 2.5%. The cap is used here as a common reference point every board in town already uses — it is not a ceiling anybody breached.
